<reason>Both sides fought a genuinely narrow, well-focused clash. A's route was logically clean: a universal "never" falls to one justified bounded pause, and A adapted well after B exposed that its opening example (an account takeover) was a payment-channel hold where the beneficiary is the victim, not the accused — A rebuilt it into a stolen-identity claimant case that does sit inside the motion, and gave direct answers to B's alternatives (hold the run harms innocents; verification takes the disputed interval; verified channels don't establish entitlement). A also landed a real symmetry point: PRO cannot treat mandatory review as enforceable while calling mandatory restoration fiction. But A's entire case rests on one engineered hypothetical with no grounding beyond assertion, and B named that limitation squarely. B did more comparative work with better-anchored material (Dutch childcare benefits, Robodebt, Michigan) used cautiously and to real effect: "bounded pause" and "provisional" were precisely the legal forms the disasters took, so A's safeguards are the same promises that were abandoned. B's strongest and least-answered move was the capacity dilemma — an agency that can supply reasons, a live hardship line and automatic restoration within the hour could have had someone look at the file, while the agency that truly cannot spare a reviewer is the one whose expiry clock quietly slips. A's answer (capacity before disbursement differs from capacity across the review window) is reasonable but does not dissolve the scale worry, which is the right frame for a rule addressed to public agencies. B also pressed the textual point that A's own safeguards amount to meaningful human review, forcing A into "haggling over minutes"; A's rejoinder that the suspension itself was caused solely by the flag is coherent, so this stays contested rather than decisive. Both handled pressure questions with proper A1:/A2: labels and without evasion. B carries an execution cost for two clipped overlong turns, but retains the clearer, better-weighted reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's twin hits: first showing A's opening example was a payment-channel hold in which the beneficiary is a victim rather than a flagged suspect, forcing A to rebuild its central case; then the capacity dilemma — the exception is safe only where it is unnecessary and necessary only where it will not be honoured — which converted A's own safeguard list into evidence against it and was never fully neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
